disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by at least one lifetime manic episode, typically lasting at least one week and causing marked impairment in social or occupational functioning, often requiring hospitalization. Manic episodes involve a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy or activity, frequently accompanied by inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, and risky or goal-directed behaviors. Depressive episodes are common but not required for the diagnosis, and the course is often recurrent with variable periods of remission between episodes. It is distinguished from Bipolar II Disorder by the presence of full mania rather than hypomania, and from primary psychotic disorders by the episodic nature of mood symptoms and their temporal relationship to any psychotic features.

narrative.personality: Lyman is a steady, routine-driven handyman who values community, church, and hands-on projects like classic car restoration and gardening.
narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Lyman’s part-time home-maintenance work in Oak Hill steadily dried up as a larger franchise moved into town and several long-time clients either moved away or shifted to cheaper services, leaving him feeling pushed out of a role that had defined his identity for decades. Already out of the formal workforce and proud of being the dependable “go-to guy” for neighbors and the volunteer fire department, he reacted to the loss of steady jobs by throwing himself into bigger and bigger projects on his old Chevy and around the house, determined to prove he could still build something impressive. As the months went on, his days and then his nights became consumed by increasingly ambitious repair schemes, volunteer event plans, and home projects, crowding out sleep, regular meals, and his usual fishing and church routines, while financial strain and tension with his spouse grew. When he began missing fire department workshops, clashing with his wife over large, unplanned purchases of car parts, and neighbors noticed he seemed “wired” and hadn’t slept in days, his pastor and spouse convinced him to see a doctor, leading to psychiatric referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: I barely sleep more than a couple hours a night lately and still wake up feeling like I’ve got enough energy to keep going all day and all night.

narrative.personality: Lisandra is a fiercely imaginative and competitive visual artist who thrives on novelty, creative risk-taking, and loosely structured days filled with art, music, and exploration.
narrative.stressor: Lisandra’s episode began after she landed a small gallery show and a promising meeting with an agent, which she interpreted as her breakthrough moment in the Los Angeles art world. Determined not to miss the opportunity, she started stacking multiple ambitious projects—night-sky photography series, mixed-media collages, experimental cooking pop-ups, and grant applications—on top of her usual freelance work, telling herself she could outwork anyone in her field. Over several months, she increasingly reorganized her entire life around nonstop creative production and networking, taking on shoots at all hours, packing her calendar with events and collaborations, and brushing off her partner’s concerns about her relentless pace and erratic follow-through. When she began missing client deadlines despite working almost around the clock, lost a couple of key contracts, and had a heated argument with her spouse after impulsively committing to an expensive studio rental she couldn’t afford, her partner and a close friend from yoga urged her to seek help, leading her to a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve been going nonstop with projects for months, like I’m constantly switched on and can’t slow myself down.

narrative.personality: Miguel is a laid-back but seasoned kitchen supervisor who combines curiosity for new recipes with a pragmatic, steady approach to keeping his team and restaurant running smoothly.
narrative.stressor: Miguel’s difficulties started after his divorce was finalized and his adult children moved farther away for work, leaving him living alone for the first time in decades while also being promoted to oversee a second kitchen location. On paper the promotion was a recognition of his experience, but the combination of longer hours, commuting between sites, and coming home to an empty apartment disrupted the familiar routines that had anchored him. He coped by throwing himself into work—experimenting with new menu ideas, volunteering for extra shifts, and staying late to mentor younger cooks—then filling his off-hours with car restoration, community cooking workshops, and late-night soccer games on TV, rarely allowing himself downtime. Over seven months, his days blurred into one another, with colleagues noting he seemed to function on almost no rest and was increasingly hard to redirect when he fixated on new ideas, until a concerned manager and a cousin noticed how worn but “wired” he looked and persuaded him to see his primary care doctor, who referred him to psychiatry.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’m only sleeping a few hours a night but I still feel like I can just keep going, and my family is worried it’s not normal.
